classification.difficultyReason: Adapt the supplied proof structure to coprime residues, justify their permutation under multiplication and establish that the product can be cancelled modulo a composite integer.

content.prompt: Prove Euler’s Theorem by adapting the proof of Fermat’s Little Theorem.

answer.short:
$a^{\phi(n)}\equiv1\pmod n$ when $\gcd(a,n)=1$.

Multiplication by $a$ permutes the residues coprime to $n$; equate their products and cancel the invertible factors.
answer.worked:
Let $a$ and $n$ be coprime positive integers. For $n=1$ the congruence holds trivially. For $n>1$, let $r_1,\ldots,r_{\phi(n)}$ be the distinct residues between 1 and $n-1$ that are coprime to $n$.

Each $ar_i$ is coprime to $n$. If $ar_i\equiv ar_j\pmod n$, multiplication by the inverse of $a$ gives $r_i\equiv r_j\pmod n$, so $i=j$. Hence multiplication by $a$ permutes these residues.

Put $P=r_1r_2\cdots r_{\phi(n)}$. Equating the products gives

$$\begin{align*}(ar_1)(ar_2)\cdots(ar_{\phi(n)})&\equiv P\pmod n\\a^{\phi(n)}P&\equiv P\pmod n.\end{align*}$$

Every factor of $P$ is coprime to $n$, so $P$ has an inverse modulo $n$. Cancelling $P$ gives $a^{\phi(n)}\equiv1\pmod n$, as required.
